concept.body: Arc measure (degrees) and arc length (distance) are different quantities linked by a fraction: a θ-degree arc is θ/360 of the circle, so its length is (θ/360) · 2πr. Recall C = 2πr from Grade 7. The trig course's s = rθ (radians) is the same formula with the fraction absorbed into the angle unit.

explanationVariants: A 90° arc is a quarter of the circle: (1/4)(2π · 8) = 4π ≈ 12.57.

commonErrors.feedback: 50.27 ≈ 16π is the whole circumference — the arc takes a quarter: ≈ 12.57.

steps.body: Arc MEASURE counts degrees; arc LENGTH measures distance — and the bridge is a fraction. An arc of θ degrees claims θ/360 of the circle, so it claims that same fraction of the circumference (2πr, from your Grade 7 circle work): **arc length = (θ/360) · 2πr**. Degrees price the share; the radius prices the whole.
A sixth of the way around.

widget.prompt: Radius 9, arc measure 60°. Find the arc LENGTH (2 decimals; use π ≈ 3.14159).

commonErrors.feedback: 60 is the arc's degree MEASURE — its length takes 1/6 of the 18π circumference: 3π ≈ 9.42.
56.55 ≈ 18π is the WHOLE circumference — the arc claims only 60/360 of it: ≈ 9.42.
4.71 ≈ 1.5π halves the answer — the fraction is 60/360 = 1/6, not 1/12: ≈ 9.42.

widget.prompt: Radius 12, arc measure 150°. Arc length (2 decimals) = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 75.4 ≈ 24π is the full circumference — take the 150/360 share: 10π ≈ 31.42.
150 is degrees — convert to distance via the fraction: (150/360)(24π) ≈ 31.42.
15.71 ≈ 5π uses radius 6 or halves — with r = 12 the share is 10π ≈ 31.42.

steps.body: The trigonometry course prices the same arc as **s = rθ** with θ in radians — and the two formulas are one. Convert 60° = π/3 rad: s = 9 · π/3 = 3π, exactly the fraction route's answer. Radians BUILD the fraction into the angle unit; degrees keep it explicit. Same arc, two bookkeeping systems.

explanationVariants: Fraction route: (90/360)(2π · 4) = 2π. Radian route: 90° = π/2, s = 4(π/2) = 2π. Same ≈ 6.28.
Both systems price the quarter-circle at 2π ≈ 6.28.

widget.prompt: Radius 4, arc 90°. Compute the arc length by EITHER route (2 decimals) — they must agree.

commonErrors.feedback: 12.57 ≈ 4π doubles — the quarter share of 8π is 2π ≈ 6.28 (and s = 4 · π/2 agrees).
90 is the degree measure — the length is 2π ≈ 6.28 by both routes.

steps.body: An arc is a fraction of the way round.

predict.prompt: A 60° arc sits in a circle of radius 6. What fraction of the whole circumference is it?

options.label: One sixth — because 60° is one sixth of 360°
It depends on the radius as well as the angle
60/360 of the DIAMETER rather than the circumference

predict.reveal: One sixth, and the radius never enters the fraction. An arc is the same share of the circumference that its angle is of the full turn — (1/6)(12π) = 2π. Open the angle and watch the fraction track the angle alone.

widget.prompt: Radius 6. Open the angle to 60° and read the arc length.
widget.successFeedback: 60° is one sixth of the turn, so the arc is one sixth of the circumference: (1/6)(12π) = 2π ≈ 6.28. There is no arc-length formula to memorise — there is a fraction of a lap, and the fraction is the angle over 360.
widget.lowFeedback: Not far enough round — the arc is still shorter than a sixth of the circle.
widget.highFeedback: Too far round — you have passed 60°.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate circle measurements while tangent, chord, radius, and power relationships update together.

widget.prompt: A running track's curve is a semicircle of radius 30 m. How far does the curve carry you (2 decimals)?

commonErrors.feedback: 188.5 ≈ 60π is the FULL circle — a semicircle takes half: 30π ≈ 94.25 m.
30 m is the radius — the semicircular path is (180/360)(2π · 30) = 30π ≈ 94.25 m.

hints: The fraction formula runs in reverse: 8π = (θ/360)(2π · 15).
The circumference is 30π; what fraction of it is 8π?

widget.prompt: A circle has radius 15, and an arc on it has length 8π. Find the arc's degree measure.

commonErrors.feedback: 25.13 ≈ 8π is the arc LENGTH — the measure asks degrees: (8π/30π)(360) = 96°.
192 doubles — the circumference is 2π(15) = 30π, not 15π: fraction 8/30, so 96°.

takeaways: Arc length = (θ/360) · 2πr — the degree share of the circumference.
It agrees exactly with trig's s = rθ (radians build the fraction into the unit).
Linear in BOTH θ and r; runs backward to find any missing piece.
